title: The Padlock

post.author: u/overnight_rx_mina
post.title: I fill online prescription orders overnight. At midnight our website stopped being us.

blocks.text: I'm the overnight technician at Larkspur Pharmacy, the 24-hour one across from the hospital. Online refill orders print behind the counter all night, and I fill them for morning pickup. A normal night is forty to sixty orders.
Last night the printer went quiet at 11:58 PM. At 12:20 AM the phone rang.
"Your website says you're pretending to be yourselves," said Mrs. Okafor. She has ordered her husband's heart pills from us every month for six years.

I opened larkspurrx.com in the web browser, the app you visit websites with, on the counter computer. A full red page: *Your connection is not private. Attackers might be trying to steal your information.* Next to our address there is normally a little padlock. It means what you send is scrambled on the way, so nobody in between can read it. Usually it goes in three steps. First the browser and the website agree on a secret code for the visit. Then the browser checks the website's proof of who it is. Only then does it send anything. The padlock was gone. Same on my phone. Same on the hospital Wi-Fi, its wireless internet. Not one customer. Everyone.
Our refill app, the program customers install on their phones, didn't show a warning at all. It has no page to show one on. It just said *Something went wrong* and kept spinning.

I clicked the warning for details. It showed a small file our website hands every browser to prove who it is, like an ID card. That file is called a certificate. Its lines show who the card is for, which company vouched for it, the day it started, the day it ends, and the browser's code name for the error:

subject     larkspurrx.com
issued by   Northgate Trust CA
valid from  Mon 6 Oct 2025, 00:00
expires     Tue 6 Oct 2026, 00:00
error       NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID
Our name. The same company vouching for us. Nothing about us had changed except the date.
At 3 AM I found an index card taped inside the cupboard that holds our server, the computer that runs our website. It was in the handwriting of Dev, who built our site and left in April.

Nobody has opened Dev's mailbox since he left. The password was on the back of the card. Four unread emails from Northgate, the company that vouches for our card, all with one subject line: *Your certificate for larkspurrx.com expires in 30 days.* Then 14. Then 7. Then 1.
Somebody had been warning us for a month. Every warning went to a man who doesn't work here anymore.

Thirty-one people called before 6 AM. One man said he clicked *proceed anyway* and typed in his card number. The owner will buy a new certificate when the office opens. Then what? Set an alarm for next October? And why does the browser call us attackers, when the only thing that changed was the calendar?

blocks.label: certificate_check.png

diagram.aria: What the browser checked at 12:20 AM on Tuesday 6 October. On the left, the certificate chain: Northgate Root, which is in the browser's list of trusted roots, signed Northgate Trust CA, which signed the certificate for larkspurrx.com, issued 6 October 2025 and expiring 6 October 2026 at 00:00. On the right, the browser's three checks: the signer is trusted, yes. The name matches, yes. Still in date, no, it expired 20 minutes ago.

blocks.caption: I drew what the browser checked at 12:20 AM. Our card is vouched for by Northgate's middle card, which is vouched for by Northgate's top card, called a root. The browser already trusts that root. It checks in order: first it follows the vouching up to the root, then it compares the name on the card with the address, then it compares the card's dates with its own clock. That chain still holds, and the name still matches. Only the date fails, and one failed check is enough for the red page.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Read your log again. Who it's for: still you. Who signed it, the company's stamp saying it checked you: still them. The only line that changed has a date on it. A padlock is a promise with an end date, and someone built it that way on purpose. Ask why.

replies.author: u/overnight_rx_mina
replies.text: So a fake one can't stay good forever? I'm a pharmacy tech. Until tonight I thought the padlock just came with the website.

comments.author: u/rack_rat_wendell
comments.text: Quick glossary, since nobody gave you one. HTTP is the language browsers and websites use to ask for pages and send them back. HTTPS is the same HTTP, but encrypted: scrambled on the way so only the two ends can read it. The scrambling is done by a layer called TLS, short for Transport Layer Security. Think of it as a locked tunnel. Your certificate proves the tunnel really leads to larkspurrx.com. Some companies are trusted by every browser to check that you really control your name, then sign your certificate. Each is called a certificate authority, or CA. Northgate is one. There are free ones too, like Let's Encrypt. There, a small program on your server renews the certificate by itself, fetching a fresh one every couple of months. It follows a shared set of rules called ACME. Each renewal usually goes: the program asks the CA for a new certificate, proves you still control the name by putting up something the CA asks for, collects the signed certificate, then tells the website to start using it. No index cards.

comments.author: u/night_nurse_pell
comments.text: Mine went red at 11:46 PM. Fourteen minutes before yours. My laptop clock runs fourteen minutes fast, on purpose, so I'm never late for shift.

comments.author: u/third_party_tom
comments.text: Tell the man who clicked *proceed anyway* to call his bank tonight. Your site was probably fine. But that button is exactly what someone pretending to be you would want him to press.

reply.prompt: The owner wants to make sure the padlock never breaks again. What should she do? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Buy the longest certificate on sale, five or ten years if possible, so this happens once a decade.
options.part2: The owner called three certificate companies. All three said the same thing: no certificate for a public website can last longer than 200 days now, and the limit keeps shrinking. She bought a 200-day one and wrote the new date on Dev's index card. In April the printer went quiet at midnight again. This time I knew what the red page meant. Knowing didn't make it go away.
options.senior: Browser makers and certificate authorities cut how long a certificate may last, on purpose: 200 days since March 2026, 100 days from March 2027, 47 days from March 2029. Long certificates are gone. The only lasting fix is to stop renewing by hand.

options.text: Renew by hand, but send reminders to a shared inbox, with alarms 30, 14 and 7 days before the end.
options.part2: We pointed the reminders at the shared inbox and set the alarms. In late March the 30-day alarm went off. The owner was on holiday, the relief pharmacist thought I handled it, and I thought the owner did. On day 7 I called Northgate myself, paid with my own card, and spent two hours on hold learning how to install it. The padlock held. Barely.
options.senior: A shared inbox beats one person's mailbox, but it still depends on a human acting: twice a year now, and more often every year as certificates get shorter lives. Reminders tell you about a problem. They don't fix it.

options.text: Post a notice: the warning is harmless, and customers may click *proceed anyway* until it is fixed.
options.verdict: Teaches customers to ignore the alarm
options.part2: The owner posted the notice on our page and people clicked through. Two weeks later, long after the new certificate was in, a man on the hospital café Wi-Fi got the same red page on our site. He remembered the notice and clicked through. This time it wasn't an expired certificate. Someone on that Wi-Fi was pretending to be us.
options.senior: The browser can't tell an expired certificate from a fake one held by someone pretending to be you, so it shows the same alarm for both. Teaching people to click past it trains them to ignore the one warning that protects them from a real attack.

options.text: Let a program renew it with ACME, like Let's Encrypt; a separate check warns the team at 20 days.
options.part2: Wendell from the comments set it up on Saturday. A small program on our server now renews the certificate by itself once two thirds of its life has passed, or sooner if the certificate authority's ARI says so. ARI, short for ACME Renewal Information, is a note the CA publishes for each certificate saying when it should be renewed. A separate checking service, called a monitor, looks at the live site every night and emails the pharmacy's shared inbox if fewer than 20 days are left. Nobody has touched it since. Last night the monitor emailed anyway. Not about larkspurrx.com. About old-orders.larkspurrx.com, 12 days left. None of us knew it existed. Dev's again. Still running somewhere, still answering, still counting down.
options.senior: Let a program do the renewing, then watch the result separately, because automatic jobs fail quietly. Check the certificate the live site actually hands out, not just the renewal program. Keep a list of every certificate you own, and send alerts to a team, never to one person.

sim.title: Watch the padlock checks
sim.lede: You're the pharmacy. Each dot is one customer connecting to larkspurrx.com: a browser, with a person looking at it, or the refill app, a program with no page to show. The clock runs 60 times faster than real life and starts 15 minutes before the certificate expires. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Watch the date check fail at midnight. Browsers show the red page, the app just fails. Renew by hand and see how many days you bought. Then reset, turn on auto-renew and skip ahead 30 days at a time. Finally, with auto-renew still on, install the certificate for the wrong name and see what automation can't fix.

explain.oneLine: Nobody attacked Larkspur. Its certificate, the digital ID card that proves the site is really larkspurrx.com, reached its end date at midnight, and browsers refuse a card they can no longer trust.

steps.title: HTTPS is HTTP inside a locked tunnel.
steps.text: HTTP is the language browsers and websites use to ask for pages and send them back. Plain HTTP travels like a postcard: anyone along the way, such as whoever runs a café's Wi-Fi, can read it or change it. HTTPS sends the same HTTP through TLS, a protective layer that gives three things. Privacy: the data is encrypted, scrambled so only the two ends can read it. Integrity: any change on the way is noticed. Identity: the browser can tell it is really talking to larkspurrx.com. The padlock means all three are in place.

steps.title: Identity comes from a certificate and a chain of signatures.
steps.text: TLS uses a pair of matched keys. One is kept secret by the server, so it is called the private key. The other can be handed to anyone, so it is called the public key. Anything stamped with the private key can be checked with the public one. Stamping, called signing, goes in two steps. First the owner uses the private key to make a stamp from the exact data. Then anyone with the public key checks that the stamp fits that data; if even one letter changed, it no longer fits. A certificate is a small file that says: this public key belongs to larkspurrx.com, from this date until that date. A certificate authority (CA), a company browsers trust, signs it after checking that Larkspur controls the name. Browsers and operating systems (the core software of a computer or phone) come with a short list of top-level certificates they trust, called roots. A root signs a middle certificate, called an intermediate. The intermediate signs the site's certificate. The browser follows those signatures up to a root it already knows, like checking a reference's reference. First it checks the site's certificate against the intermediate's public key. Then it checks the intermediate against the root's public key. Then it looks the root up in its own list. If a signature doesn't fit, or the server forgot to send the intermediate, or the root isn't on the list, the check fails. That trail of signatures is the chain of trust.

steps.title: The TLS handshake checks the certificate before the request goes out.
steps.text: First comes the TCP handshake, the three-message greeting that opens a connection: the browser asks to connect, the server agrees, and the browser confirms. If the server never answers, nothing else happens. Right after it comes the TLS handshake, TLS's own greeting. In TLS 1.3, the current version, the browser says hello, lists what it supports and sends half of a secret recipe. That half is called a key share. The server's hello carries the server's half. From those two halves both sides work out the same fresh keys for this one conversation, called session keys. So everything after the hellos is encrypted. If the two sides share no version or method, the handshake stops here. Then the server sends its certificate chain, already encrypted. It proves it holds the matching private key by signing the handshake. An impostor with a copied certificate but no private key fails here. Then it sends Finished, a seal over the whole exchange. The browser runs three checks: does the chain end at a trusted root, does the name match the address, and is the time now between the certificate's two dates? If all pass, the browser sends its own Finished and the HTTP request goes through encrypted. If any check fails, a browser shows a warning page and an app simply gives up.

steps.title: At 00:00 the date check started failing for everyone.
steps.text: Larkspur's certificate was valid from 6 October 2025 until 6 October 2026 at 00:00. Nothing about the server changed at midnight. Every browser compared that end date with its own clock and refused. A browser can't tell an expired certificate from a forged one, so it shows the same alarm it shows for an impostor, someone pretending to be the site. The night nurse saw it 14 minutes early because her laptop's clock runs 14 minutes fast.

steps.title: Expiry is a feature, and lifetimes keep shrinking.
steps.text: If a private key leaks, or a certificate is issued by mistake, a short life limits how long it can be misused. So the rules keep cutting how long a certificate may last. Certificates for public websites could last 398 days until March 2026. Now the limit is 200 days, from March 2027 it is 100 days, and from March 2029 just 47. At that pace, renewing by hand stops being a chore and becomes a guaranteed outage, a time when the service is down. That is why ACME, the standard way for a program to renew certificates, exists.

diagram.aria: The TLS 1.3 handshake between a browser and the pharmacy server. After the TCP handshake, the browser and the server each send a hello carrying a key share, and from the two shares both sides make the same session keys, so everything after the hellos is encrypted. The server sends its certificate chain, then proof that it holds the private key and its Finished message. The browser checks chain, name and date, sends its own Finished, and only then do the encrypted request and response flow. Outcome: from 00:00 on 6 October the date check fails and the browser shows a red warning page.

steps.text: From 00:00: date check fails, red page

explain.caption: Read top to bottom. The TCP handshake from case 3, the greeting that opens a connection, comes first. Then TLS 1.3: two hellos, each carrying half of the key recipe. After them everything is scrambled, the certificate included. The server proves it holds the private key, the browser runs its three checks and sends Finished, and only then does the request go. From 00:00 on Tuesday the third check, the date, failed, so every customer's conversation stopped at the checks.

fix.title: The fix: automate renewal, then watch it separately
fix.text: Use ACME, the standard set of rules certificate authorities use to issue certificates with no human involved. A small program on the server that speaks ACME, called an ACME client, does the work. (Many hosting and cloud companies, which rent out servers, offer built-in certificates that do the same.) It proves to the CA that you control the name, usually by publishing a file or a DNS record the CA asks for. A DNS record is an entry in the internet's phone book. Then it fetches the new certificate and restarts the website so it uses it. Each step can fail: a blocked proof, a failed fetch, or a website that keeps using the old file. Let's Encrypt, a free CA, issues 90-day certificates today. It will cut that to 64 days in February 2027 and 45 days in February 2028, so don't renew on a fixed timer such as every 60 days. Renew once about two thirds of the certificate's life has passed, or when ARI, the CA's own renewal hint for each certificate, says to. Then add an independent monitor, a separate program that checks the certificate the live site actually hands out. Usually it connects to the site the way a browser would, reads the end date on the certificate it gets, and alerts a shared team channel when fewer than, say, 20 days remain. Keep a list of every certificate you own, with an owner for each. Include old subdomains, names under yours like old-orders.larkspurrx.com.

limits: Automatic jobs fail quietly. A firewall change (a firewall is a filter that blocks some traffic), a DNS change, or a server that never reloads the new file can stop renewals with nobody noticing. That is why the separate monitor matters. It is also why Let's Encrypt, which stopped sending expiry reminder emails in June 2025, tells people to monitor instead.

A padlock proves the name, not the business. A CA checks that you control larkspurrx.com, not that you're an honest pharmacy. So a scam site with a look-alike name can have a perfect padlock. And TLS protects data only on the way: it does nothing for a hacked server or the data stored on it.

Some trust is out of your hands. Old devices carry old lists of trusted roots. A wrong clock on a customer's laptop breaks the date check from their side, as the night nurse saw. And when a root itself expires, devices that never got the newer root show warnings on sites that did nothing wrong.

head: How you renew
Good
Bad
rows: 200 days now and falling. Someone must remember, and people leave.
ACME client (renewal program) on your own server
You run and update the program, and it can fail without telling anyone, so you still need a monitor.
Managed by your cloud or hosting company
Renews itself for the services they run, such as AWS (Amazon Web Services) load balancers (servers that share visitors across other servers).
Covers only what they host. Certificates you bring in yourself or copy elsewhere are still yours to renew.

explain.seniorTake: Certificates don't fail. Calendars do. Treat every certificate as a timer that is already running. Let one machine renew it, let a different machine watch the live site, and send the alarm to a team, never to one person's inbox.

realWorld.title: Microsoft Teams, February 3, 2020
realWorld.text: TechCrunch reported Teams, Microsoft's workplace chat and meetings app, down from about 8:30 AM US Eastern time on a Monday. Around 10 AM, Microsoft's status account posted that it had "determined that an authentication certificate has expired causing users to have issues using the service" and that it was developing a fix to apply a new certificate. An authentication certificate is one a service uses to prove who it is, for example when signing people in. Microsoft then began putting the updated certificate in place. The status posts didn't say which certificate it was or why it lapsed. One expired certificate was enough to lock users out.

realWorld.title: Let's Encrypt: short on purpose
realWorld.text: Let's Encrypt, a free certificate authority, has issued 90-day certificates from the start. In 2015 it gave two reasons: short lifetimes limit the damage from stolen keys and from certificates issued by mistake, and they encourage automation, which it called absolutely essential.

realWorld.title: Let's Encrypt: 45 days by 2028
realWorld.text: In December 2025 Let's Encrypt announced it will move its default certificates to 64 days in February 2027 and 45 days in February 2028. Its advice: let your ACME client, the renewal program, renew automatically. It should renew at about two thirds of the certificate's life if it can't use ACME Renewal Information, the CA's per-certificate hint. Don't renew by hand, and monitor so you hear when a renewal fails. It warns that renewing at a hardcoded interval of 60 days, a fixed timer written into the setup, will no longer be sufficient.

realWorld.title: The industry's schedule
realWorld.text: In April 2025 the CA/Browser Forum, the group of certificate authorities and browser makers that writes the rules every public certificate follows, voted to shrink the longest a certificate may last. Its rulebook, called the Baseline Requirements, now sets 200 days for certificates issued from March 15, 2026, 100 days from March 15, 2027, and 47 days from March 15, 2029. Before that the limit was 398 days, which is how Larkspur's October 2025 certificate could last a full year.

realWorld.title: When a root expires: September 30, 2021
realWorld.text: Trust has dates at the top of the chain too. For years, Let's Encrypt certificates were also vouched for by an older, better-known root, DST Root CA X3. One CA's root signing for another like this is called a cross-sign. It meant devices that didn't yet know Let's Encrypt's own root, ISRG Root X1, still trusted them. When that cross-sign expired on September 30, 2021, older devices that didn't trust ISRG Root X1 started getting certificate warnings on sites that had done nothing wrong.

asked: What happens when you visit an https:// website?
A certificate expired and took production down. How do you make sure it never happens again?
interview.answer: Walk the layers in order. DNS, the phone book, turns the name into an IP address. TCP opens the connection with its handshake. Then comes the TLS handshake. In TLS 1.3 the two hellos carry key shares, so both sides have session keys after one round trip, one message there and one back. Everything after that is encrypted. The server's certificate chain and its proof of the private key arrive encrypted. The client checks three things: the chain up to a trusted root, the hostname (the name in the address), and the dates. Both sides send Finished, and HTTP runs encrypted inside. For the outage: automate getting and renewing certificates with ACME, or a managed service such as AWS Certificate Manager. Renew at about two thirds of the lifetime or when ARI says, never on a fixed timer. Monitor the certificate each live endpoint (each address clients connect to) actually serves, with alerts going to a team well before expiry. Keep an inventory of every certificate, with an owner. Name the limits before they ask: automation can fail silently, lifetimes are shrinking to 47 days by 2029, and customers' clocks and trust stores (their lists of trusted roots) are outside your control.

terms.def: The lock icon next to a web address: the TLS checks passed, so the connection is encrypted and the site proved its name. Chrome shows a "tune" icon there instead since version 117 (September 2023).
HTTP sent through TLS. The same requests and responses as HTTP, but encrypted, protected from changes, and with the site's identity checked. Addresses start with https://.
Transport Layer Security: the protective layer that scrambles a connection, notices any change on the way and proves the server is who it says. HTTPS is HTTP running inside TLS.
Secure Sockets Layer, the older set of rules TLS replaced. People still say "SSL certificate" when they mean a TLS certificate.
Scrambling data with a key so that only someone holding the right key can read it.
What TLS's encryption gives you: people between you and the site, like whoever runs a café's Wi-Fi, can see that you connected but not what you sent or received.
Knowing data wasn't changed on the way. TLS detects any change in transit and drops the connection.
Proof that you're talking to the real owner of the name. In TLS the server shows its certificate and proves it holds the matching private key.
A small signed file, a website's ID card. It names the site, holds its public key, and says from when until when it's valid. A certificate authority signs it.
CA for short. An organisation browsers trust to check that whoever asks for a certificate really controls the name, and then to sign it. Let's Encrypt is a free one.
One of a matched pair of keys, safe to hand to anyone. With it, anyone can check a stamp made with the matching private key.
The secret one of a matched pair of keys. The server keeps it and uses it to prove it owns its certificate. If it leaks, anyone holding it can pretend to be the site.
A stamp made with a private key that anyone can check with the matching public key. It proves who signed and that nothing changed since.
A CA's top-level certificate, built into browsers and operating systems. It's trusted without anyone vouching for it, and its private key is kept locked away, off the internet.
A certificate signed by a root, which a CA uses day to day to sign websites' certificates, so the root's key can stay locked away.
The path of signatures from a site's certificate, through an intermediate, up to a root the browser already trusts. If a link is missing or wrong, the check fails.
The list of root certificates a browser or operating system trusts. Old devices have old lists.
The name in the address, like larkspurrx.com. The certificate must cover that exact name, or the browser refuses it.
A name under your domain, like old-orders.larkspurrx.com. Each one needs a certificate that covers it, and each one can expire on its own.
The "not after" date in a certificate. From that moment on, browsers and apps treat it as invalid, even if nothing else changed.

The short exchange at the start of a TLS connection: two hellos that set up session keys, then the server's certificate and proof, the client's checks, and Finished. It comes right after the TCP handshake.
The current version of TLS, written down in RFC 8446 (2018), a numbered internet standard. Its handshake takes one message each way, and everything after the two hellos is encrypted.
In TLS 1.3, each side's half of a key exchange, sent in its hello. From the two halves both sides compute the same session keys, and the keys themselves never cross the network.
Fresh, temporary keys both sides work out from the two key shares in the hellos, and use to encrypt the rest of that one conversation.
The last TLS handshake message from each side: a seal over the whole handshake that proves both sides saw the same messages and hold the same keys.
The full-page alarm a browser shows when a TLS check fails, such as "Your connection is not private." You can click past it, and almost never should.
A certificate signed by its own key instead of a CA. No chain leads to a trusted root, so browsers reject it.
What a CA does when it creates and signs a certificate for someone. The site owner then installs it on their server.
Getting a new certificate for the same name before the old one expires, and installing it on the server.
The HTTP request type for reading, as in GET /refills: "send me the refills page". It asks for something without changing it.
What the server sends back to a request: a status code such as 200 OK, headers (labelled notes about the reply), and usually a body, like the page itself.
The status code, the number a server's answer starts with, for a request that worked.
One address that clients connect to, such as larkspurrx.com or api.larkspurrx.com. Each one presents its own certificate.
Automatic Certificate Management Environment: the standard set of rules (RFC 8555) a server uses to prove it controls a name and get or renew a certificate with no human involved.
The small program on a server that speaks ACME: on a schedule it proves control of the name, fetches the new certificate and installs it.
ARI for short. A way for a CA to tell ACME clients when to renew each certificate, so renewals happen at the right moment, or early if the CA needs them to.
A free, non-profit certificate authority that issues certificates only through ACME. Its default certificates last 90 days in 2026, falling to 45 days by 2028.
How a CA checks you control a name: it asks you to publish a specific file on the site or a specific DNS record, then looks for it.
Checking a system automatically and often, and raising an alert when something looks wrong, such as a certificate with fewer than 20 days left.
A filter that decides which network traffic may pass. A new firewall rule can block the CA's validation check and quietly stop renewals.
When a private key leaks or is stolen. Whoever has it can pretend to be the site until the certificate expires or is cancelled.
To cancel a certificate before its expiry date, for example after its private key leaks.
Here, a server pretending to be a site it isn't, such as an attacker on shared Wi-Fi answering in the real site's place. TLS's checks are what stop it.
The group of certificate authorities and browser makers that sets the rules all public certificates follow, including how long they may last.
The CA/Browser Forum's rulebook for public TLS certificates. It sets, among other things, the longest a certificate may be valid.
When one CA's root signs another CA's certificate, so devices that trust the first also trust the second. New CAs use it until their own root is widely known.
Microsoft's chat and video meetings app for workplaces.
A certificate a service uses to prove its identity, for example when signing users in or when its own parts talk to each other. When it expires, those checks fail.
A server that receives incoming visitors and shares them out across several servers behind it, like a host seating diners. On AWS it often holds the site's certificate.
Amazon's content delivery network: servers around the world that keep copies of your site near users and serve it over HTTPS with your certificate.
One of AWS's geographic areas, a group of data centers in one part of the world. Many services, ACM certificates included, live separately in each Region.
ACM for short. Amazon's certificate service. It issues free public certificates for AWS services and renews them itself; certificates you import, you renew yourself.
Amazon's monitoring service. It stores measurements over time, called metrics, such as a certificate's days to expiry, and can raise alarms when they cross a line.
Amazon's event service. It delivers events, such as "certificate approaching expiration", to whatever you connect, like an email or a ticket.

atWork: Open the AWS console, the website for managing your company's Amazon Web Services account. Go to AWS Certificate Manager (ACM), Amazon's certificate service. Do this in each Region your team uses (a Region is one of Amazon's areas of data centers, and each keeps its own list). Sort the certificates by expiry date. For each one, check how it got there. If ACM issued it with DNS validation (proving the name through a DNS record), ACM renews it itself while a service such as a load balancer or CloudFront is using it. If someone imported it, brought it in from outside, ACM never renews it; a person or a script must. Then look for an alert. That could be a CloudWatch alarm (Amazon's monitoring service) on the DaysToExpiry metric, the count of days left. Or it could be a rule in EventBridge, Amazon's service that passes news of events along, on the "ACM Certificate Approaching Expiration" event. Either should alert a team rather than one person. Finally, list the certificates that live outside AWS, such as on old servers and subdomains, and give each one an owner.

recall.prompt: Your company's main website certificate expires in 9 days. It has been renewed by hand once a year, and the person who did it last year has left. What do you do this week, and what do you change for good?

keyIdeas.idea: Renew it now, before it expires, and check the live site serves the new one
Automate renewal with ACME or a managed service
Monitor the live certificate's expiry and alert a team, not one person

recall.model: This week: renew it by hand, install it, and check that the live site actually hands out the new certificate. For good: switch to automatic renewal, where a program does the renewing. That could be an ACME client on the server, or a managed service such as AWS Certificate Manager, renewing at about two thirds of the certificate's life. Add a separate monitor that checks the certificate the live site serves. It should alert a team channel when fewer than about 20 days remain. Keep a list of every certificate, each with an owner. Lifetimes are shrinking to 47 days by 2029, so renewing by hand won't survive anyway.

recall.prompt: At midnight every browser showed Larkspur's red warning page, though nothing on the server had changed. Which check failed?
options: The chain: the signer was no longer trusted
The name: the certificate was for a different site
The date: the certificate's expiry had passed
The server stopped answering on its port
recall.why: The chain and the name still checked out. The certificate's end date was 6 October 2026 at 00:00, and every browser compared it with its own clock.

recall.prompt: How does a browser decide whether to trust larkspurrx.com's certificate?
options: It looks up the site's IP address through DNS
It follows signatures from the site's certificate, through a middle one, up to a root it already trusts
It asks the site for a password
It checks how many years the site has existed
recall.why: That path of signatures is the chain of trust. The browser only trusts roots it already ships with, and each certificate below must be signed by the one above.

recall.prompt: A teammate says: "Our certificate renews itself with an ACME client, so we don't need any monitoring." What could still go wrong, and what do you suggest?

keyIdeas.idea: Monitor the certificate the live site actually serves
Alert a team well before expiry

recall.model: Automatic jobs fail quietly. A firewall or DNS change can block the CA's check that you own the name. The renewal program can crash or stop being run. Or the server can keep serving the old file because it never reloaded. Keep the ACME client, and add an independent monitor. It connects to the live site, reads the certificate it actually serves, and alerts a team when fewer than about 20 days remain. Take a 90-day certificate renewed once two thirds of its life has passed, about 30 days before expiry. An alert at 20 days left means renewal has been failing for 10 days, with time left to fix it. Renew at that point or when ARI says, never on a fixed 60-day timer, because lifetimes are shrinking to 64 days in 2027 and 45 in 2028. As they shrink, keep the alert line below the renewal point.

recall.prompt: Which of these does TLS NOT protect you from?
options: Someone on café Wi-Fi reading the password you send
A device along the way changing the page you receive
A scam site with a look-alike name and its own valid certificate
A server pretending to be the real larkspurrx.com
recall.why: A CA only checks that the scam site controls its own look-alike name, so its padlock is genuine. TLS proves you reached the name in the address bar, not that the name belongs to an honest business.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The website's certificate has renewed itself twice. Then last night at 2 AM the refill app stopped working, while the site loaded fine in every browser. It turns out the app talks to api.larkspurrx.com, a separate server Dev set up, with its own certificate, renewed by hand. It was on nobody's list. The owner asks how we keep finding these.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What happened, and how do you stop the next one?

keyIdeas.idea: The app's server had its own certificate, and it expired
Apps fail without a warning page, so it looks mysterious
Keep an inventory of every certificate and monitor each endpoint

coldCase.model: The website and api.larkspurrx.com are different servers with different certificates. The app's server, the API (a front desk for programs rather than people), had its own certificate. The API's certificate was renewed by hand and on nobody's list, and it expired at 2 AM. A browser would have shown a red page. But the app is a program with no page to show: its TLS check failed and it just stopped with an error, which is why it looked like a mystery. Put that server on the same automatic renewal. Then build an inventory, a full list, of every name and server that hands out a certificate, old ones included. Point the expiry monitor at all of them, alerting a team. Better still, regularly list every name in your DNS records, your entries in the internet's phone book, so new ones can't hide.
